AK1.v: The calculation below modifies load at each beam due to any change in the moment at the beam.  The moment changes when the spacing of vertical stiffeners becomes less than the critical ratio.  The moment from plate bending above and below the beam can be different so we take the moment to be the average of the two for the purposes of getting the beam load.

A3.v: Stresses for the skinplate panel closest to the center of the gate span are determined.  These stresses are combined using von-Mises theory where they are biaxial.  Bending moments for the skinplate panel are determined by flat plate bending theory if the ratio of stiffener spacing divided by panel height (b/a) is less than 2 for intermediate spaces or 4 for above the top beam and below the bottom beam.  For ratios above this value the bending moment is determined using beam spacing.  The capacity ratio for the combined stress is determined and must be no more than unity.

AD5.v: Critical b/a ratio (stiffener spacing / panel height)

A3.v: The ellipse of contact and the resultant stresses are determined for a wheel bearing on a track.  The method uses elliptic integrals as described by Skinner with Thomas & Hoersch.  The roller treads typically have a surface hardness in the range 280 to 320 BHN with the roller paths having a hardness in the range 290 to 330 BHN.  The permissible shear stress is based on the Skinner paper while the permissible compressive stress is based on DIN 19704.

A69.v: The axle bending strength is checked assuming that it is supported on each side of the wheel by vertical stiffeners on the gate.  The axle ends with a triangular pressure distribution; i.e. zero pressure on the outer edge and max pressure on inner edge.  The point of load support is therefore 1/3 of the plate thickness from the inner edge.  The wheels are loaded both radially and laterally.

A91.v: Max bearing stress from lateral load

A97.v: The end beam is checked for bending between the wheels assuming an associated width of skinplate.  Two vertical stiffeners are used to support the axle ends.

K112.v: lateral moment of inertia (ignores vertical stiffener)

K113.v: factor for lateral torsional buckling (negative for stem compression)

A121.v: The axle bending strength is checked assuming that it is cantilevered from the end of the gate.  Two support points are assumed for the wheel axle corresponding to vertical stiffeners.  This design usually results in a heavy wheel axle but has the advantage of easier wheel maintenance.  It may also economize on the space required in the gate guides.  The wheels are loaded both radially and laterally.

A143.v: Max bearing stress from lateral load

A151.v: The end beam is checked for bending between the wheels assuming an associated width of skinplate.  One vertical stiffener takes the majority of the wheel load.  An inner stiffener is required to support the inner end of the wheel axle.

K166.v: lateral moment of inertia (ignores vertical stiffener)

K167.v: factor for lateral torsional buckling (negative for stem compression)
